blocks.text: 1. HNSW
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302836-532136808.png
HNSW, the graph based algorithm behind many modern vector databases, gives the family of ANN algorithms its first concrete, widely used example.
It navigates a layered graph of connected vectors to quickly find close neighbors, a graph based approach to approximate search.
2. From The Family To A Specific Algorithm
HNSW stands for Hierarchical Navigable Small World, one specific way to implement the ANN idea.
It is widely used as the default algorithm in many popular vector databases today.
3. Building A Graph Of Neighbors
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303006-466901517.png
Each vector becomes a node connected to a handful of its nearest neighbors.
That forms a navigable graph structure instead of a flat list.
4. The Hierarchy Of Layers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303008-401228142.png
HNSW builds several layers of this graph, with fewer nodes at higher layers.
The top layer lets search take huge, coarse jumps across the whole space quickly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Layer","Node density"],"rows":[["Top layer","Sparse, few nodes, large jumps"],["Bottom layer","Dense, every node, fine grained search"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Searching Top Down
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303009-223078627.png
A search starts at the top, sparse layer and descends toward the bottom, dense layer.
Each layer refines the search closer to the actual nearest neighbors before dropping down one level.
6. Greedy Graph Traversal
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303009-178512507.png
At each layer, the algorithm greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closest to the query.
It repeats that local, greedy step until no closer neighbor exists at that layer.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Greedy traversal can occasionally settle into a locally good but not globally optimal position, which is exactly why HNSW is an approximate algorithm rather than a guaranteed exact one.

blocks.text: 7. Why HNSW Scales Well
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303010-912109255.png
HNSW searches in roughly logarithmic time instead of the linear time brute force search needs.
A collection ten times larger does not take ten times longer to search.
8. Build Time And Memory Cost
Building the graph structure takes real time and real memory, echoing the build time versus query time tradeoff covered in Indexing.
Storing those neighbor connections adds overhead beyond just the raw vectors themselves.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: An HNSW index stores not just the vectors but also every neighbor connection at every layer, meaning its memory footprint is noticeably larger than the raw vectors alone would require.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When HNSW Is A Strong Choice

blocks.alt: Recognizing When HNSW Is A Strong Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303010-445983257.png
Large collections needing fast, high recall search suit HNSW well.
Extremely memory constrained environments may prefer a lighter algorithm, covered later in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below runs a simplified single layer graph traversal that mirrors HNSW's greedy search.

code.content:
import random

def euclidean_distance(v1, v2):
    return sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) ** 0.5

def build_simple_graph(vectors, connections_per_node=4):
    # connect each node to its closest few neighbors
    graph = {}
    for i, v in enumerate(vectors):
        distances = sorted(range(len(vectors)), key=lambda j: euclidean_distance(v, vectors[j]) if j != i else float("inf"))
        graph[i] = distances[:connections_per_node]
    return graph

def greedy_search(query, vectors, graph, start_node=0):
    # repeatedly hop to whichever neighbor is closer to the query
    current = start_node
    current_dist = euclidean_distance(query, vectors[current])
    steps = 0
    while True:
        neighbors = graph[current]
        closer_found = False
        for neighbor in neighbors:
            dist = euclidean_distance(query, vectors[neighbor])
            if dist < current_dist:
                current, current_dist = neighbor, dist
                closer_found = True
        steps += 1
        if not closer_found:
            break
    return current, current_dist, steps

vectors = [[random.random() for _ in range(8)] for _ in range(200)]
query = [random.random() for _ in range(8)]

graph = build_simple_graph(vectors)
result_node, result_dist, steps = greedy_search(query, vectors, graph)

print(f"Greedy search found node {result_node} in {steps} steps")
print(f"Final distance: {result_dist:.4f}")
print("Notice the search never checked all 200 vectors directly.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the greedy traversal converging on a close match in only a handful of steps, without ever comparing the query against the full collection at once.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming HNSW guarantees the exact same result as brute force search every time.
Underestimating HNSW's memory overhead from storing graph connections alongside the raw vectors.
Using a single flat graph instead of the hierarchical, multi layer structure that gives HNSW its speed.
Ignoring HNSW's build time cost when choosing it for a rapidly changing, frequently rebuilt collection.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: HNSW navigates a layered graph of connected vectors to quickly find close neighbors.
It stands for Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a widely used default in many vector databases.
Each vector becomes a node connected to a handful of its nearest neighbors, forming a graph.
HNSW builds several layers, with fewer nodes at higher layers for coarse, fast jumps.
Search starts at the sparse top layer and descends toward the dense bottom layer.
At each layer, the algorithm greedily moves toward whichever neighbor is closest to the query.
HNSW searches in roughly logarithmic time instead of linear time, scaling well with collection size.
Building and storing the graph structure adds real memory overhead beyond the raw vectors.
